paper_title: System 1 agents: a method for local, reliable and fast agentic AI

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agentic artificial intelligence could automate analyses of sensitive clinical data, but current agents depend on large language models (LLMs). Cloud LLMs expose patient data. Local LLMs hallucinate, and an invented value in a tool call propagates through every later step. Here we present a method to build System 1 agents: local agents that call tools without generating text. A deterministic compiler turns each tool's schema and the request into multiple-choice questions whose options come from the request and the schema, then a one-pass decision model answers them. On 1,952 requests to 157 biomedical tools, the best System 1 agent chose the right tool, or correctly declined, for 97.0% of requests, significantly ahead of all 18 local LLM-agent settings (best 95.2%). The System 1 agent filled 97.0% of 6,056 stated argument values. No System 1 call contained invented content, against 5.5-19.7% of LLM calls. The System 1 Agents framework is freely available as open-source software at https://github.com/eltzanis/SystemOneAgents.

sections.title: MAIN
sections.content: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems plan and execute analyses by calling software tools 13. In clinical research and practice, such agents could prepare imaging studies, train and apply models, and query biomedical databases on request. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives tools common interface for this purpose, where each tool publishes name, description and JSON schema of its arguments 4. Two obstacles keep such agents out of clinical use. The first is privacy. The most capable language models run as cloud services, so every request and the data it refers to leave the institution. For patient data, this conflicts with data protection rules and institutional policy 5,6. Local models remove this risk, because data never leave the site 7. The second obstacle is reliability. Local language models are smaller, and an agent built on any language model writes each tool call token by token. It can call tool that does not exist, use an argument the tool lacks or fill an argument with value the user never gave 811. In an analysis pipeline, such hallucinated value does not fail visibly. It changes the result of that step, and every later step builds on it. Reasoning modes reduce some errors but multiply the text generated per call and, together with it, time and energy 12,13. Nonetheless, most of tool call is not open-ended and tools are listed in the catalogue. Almost every value 1Artificial Intelligence and Translational Imaging (ATI) Lab, Department of Radiology, School of Medicine, University of Crete, Heraklion, Crete, Greece. 2Division of Radiology, Department of Clinical Science Intervention and Technology (CLINTEC), Karolinska Institute, Huddinge, Sweden. 3Department of Medical Imaging, University Hospital of Heraklion, Crete, Greece. *Corresponding author: Eleftherios Tzanis, PhD. E-mail: eleftherios.tzanis@ki.se; etzanis@uoc.gr; tzaniseleftherios@gmail.com. ORCID: 0000-0003-0353-481X. correct call needs is written in the request, follows from it by fixed rule, such as unit conversion, or is listed in the tools schema. What remains is series of choices. Specifically, which tool, which written value for which argument, whether to call at all. Decision models are built for such choices. They read state, question and finite list of options, and return probability for each option in one forward pass 1417. Dual-process accounts of cognition call this kind of fast, single-step judgement System 1 18. Here we present method to build System 1 agents, local agents in which every decision is multiple-choice question answered by decision model, and no text is generated. We describe the architecture, the development method and the system we built with it for biomedical research. We then compare six System 1 agents with nine local LLM-based agents, in accuracy, reliability and efficiency. RESULTS method to build System 1 agents. The method rests on the principle that the model judges, and code executes verbatim what is requested. System 1 agent therefore has three components with one responsibility each (Fig. 1a): (i) the agent, (ii) the compiler and (iii) the decision model. The agent controls the workflow. It asks one question over every tool of the catalogue plus none of these. The System 1 model outputs probability score for each option. If the two most probable tools are within probability of 0.3, it queries which of the two has parameters for the values the request gives. It then asks 1 System 1 agents 2 whether the chosen tool can do what is requested, and declines below probability of 0.5. Subsequently, it passes the chosen tool and the request to the compiler. In case required value is missing, the agent does not fill it. Instead, it shows the user fixed prompt, the arguments name and its schema description, and waits for the value. When the value is present it sends the call. The prompt is template filled from the schema and no stochastic generation happens at any step. The compiler is deterministic code that turns the chosen tools JSON schema and the request into questions with finite options. An enumeration is asked over its values, boolean over on, off or not mentioned. Paths, numbers, names and other free values are asked over candidates that the compiler extracts from the request and the schema, plus not specified. Candidates include values derived by fixed rules, such as unit conversions, numbers written as words and paths composed from written parts. List items are chosen one at time, so candidates compete. An optional value is set only when the probability on the requests values reaches 0.7, and value equal to the documented default is not passed. required value that the request does not give is never filled and instead the compiler reports it to the agent as missing. The decision model answers each question with probability for every option, in one forward pass. question has four parts, state, question text, an option list and kind (choice or yes/no). Any decision model that answers this interface can be used unchanged. This division makes hallucinated content impossible by design. decision model can only pick among the options it is shown. Every tool in System 1 call therefore comes from the catalogue, every argument name from the schema and every value from the request, the schema or the agents policy. Every decision carries probability that thresholds turn into declines and prompts for missing values. On the same hardware and software, the same input gives the same output, and run can be replayed exactly from its stored answers and audited question by question. Figure 1b follows one request through these steps. We developed the compiler with loop that keeps model failures and compiler failures apart (Methods). compiler oracle, which replaces the decision model with component that knows the label, shows whether the compiler can express each labelled call. Requests the oracle cannot complete reveal values that no question offers. These are fixed by general rules about how requests write values and not by rules for particular tool. change is accepted only if it raises the summed number of correct calls across models on development requests, loses no earlier reference request beyond fixed tolerance and survives leave-one-out runs. local System 1 agent for biomedical research. We applied the method to multiple biomedical research fields (Methods). total of 157 tools of 18 MCP servers for image classification, segmentation, radiomics, AutoML, computed tomography foundation model, proteomics, metabolomics, genomics, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, clinical trials and chemistry. We used six published decision models with 4 to 35 billion parameters, without fine-tuning (Extended Data Table 1). Each ran locally on one GPU through llama.cpp. We compared the System 1 agents with nine openweight LLM-based agents, each with reasoning on and off (Extended Data Table 2). Three of the LLMs are the base models of five of the decision models. Each LLM-based agent ran as distributed, on the same GPU, with the request as the only message and every tool as native function. The evaluation set comprised 2,126 requests: 2,003 custom prompts and 123 prompts taken verbatim from published research studies 19,20. Together they contain 1,645 complete requests, which state 6,056 argument values, 307 out-of-scope requests, which no tool can serve, and 174 underspecified requests, which omit required value. All 123 published prompts are complete requests. The 1,952 complete and out-of-scope requests (1,829 custom and 123 published) form the main benchmark for accuracy; the 174 underspecified requests were evaluated separately. scorer tool was developed to judge every agent (Methods). Comparison by category. System 1 agents were more accurate in most pairwise comparisons. They never invented content and, instead of inventing missing required value, left it for the user to supply. On declining out-of-scope requests and on schema validity, the optimal LLM-agent configurations were comparable. Three of the four LLM-agent configurations that declined requests as often as System 1 agents, left 13.7-36.5% of complete requests without call. At higher accuracy, OpenJev-based System 1 agent was faster and used less energy than the best LLM-based agent configuration. On argument filling, five LLM-based agents were not significantly different from the best System 1 agent, and the cheapest LLM-based agent without reasoning, matched the cheapest System 1 agents on energy and time. Table 1 summarizes the comparison between System 1 agents and LLM-based agents. Accuracy. We measured accuracy in three ways on the main benchmark of 1,952 requests (1,645 complete and 307 out-of-scope). Tool calling, counts the requests for which the agent called the labelled tool or, when the request was out of scope, declined. Argument filling, counts the 6,056 values that the complete requests state, with value considered right only in call to the right tool. request is fully correct when its entire outcome is right. For complete request, the agent must call the labelled tool, provide all stated values correctly, and leave no required arguments empty. For an outof-scope request, the agent must decline. Values not specified in the request are not counted as errors in this System 1 agents 3 assessment, as we evaluated invented values separately (see Reliability section). The six System 1 agents reached 91.7-97.0% accuracy on tool calling, 89.8-97.0% on argument filling and 81.4-93.9% on fully correct request assessment (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Table 3). pplx-decider-27b reached 97.0%, 97.0% and 93.9% (95% confidence interval (CI) 92.7-94.8%), and OpenJev 96.1%, 96.1% and 92.9%, respectively. The best LLM-based agent, Qwen3.5-27B with reasoning off, reached 95.1%, 97.2% and 91.3% accuracy on the tool calling, argument filling and fully correct criteria, respectively. Neither reasoning setting consistently outperformed the other across LLMs. Enabling reasoning improved full correctness for five models but reduced it for four. We compared each System 1 agent with each LLMagent in each mode, 108 pairs per measure, with Holm correction  (Fig. 3)  . On fully correct requests, System 1 was significantly ahead in 73 pairs and the LLM in 11, with no significant difference in 24. pplx-decider27b-based agent was ahead of all 18 LLM-based agents and OpenJev-based agent of 17. All 11 LLM leads were over the two weakest System 1 agents. The advantage was primarily in tool selection, with System 1 agents outperforming the LLM-based agents in 76 pairs compared with just 5 pairs in which the LLM-based agents performed better. On argument filling, the larger LLMs were closer (46 System 1 leads, 19 LLM leads, 43 ties). The two pplx-decider models were ahead of their own base model run as an agent, by 2.6-9.6 percentage points on fully correct requests; decider-35b-a3b-based System 1 agent was behind its base model with reasoning on (Extended Data Table 4). By tool group, System 1 led most on medical imaging tools whose calls carry many technical values, such as nnU-Net 21, and the LLM-based agents filled values better for identifierheavy biomedical databases such as ClinicalTrials.gov and ChEMBL 22 (Extended Data Table 5). Reliability. No System 1 call contained hallucinated content (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Table 7). Across 10,888 System 1 calls, every tool and argument name was in the catalogue, and none of 33,945 argument values was ungrounded. We counted value as ungrounded when it matched neither the labelled value, nor text or number written in the request, nor an option the compiler offered for that argument, nor the tools schema. This test counts any value written anywhere in the request as grounded, so it undercounts hallucination. The LLM-based agents never called nonexistent tool, but three of the nine agents used argument names absent from the schema, in 19-53 calls per setting. total of 5.519.7% of LLM-based agent calls contained at least one invented value. Most invented values were settings the user never stated, such as hyperparameters, file paths and options. Reasoning did not remove them. System 1 agents did not guess missing values. On the 174 underspecified requests, they chose the right tool, filled the stated values and reported the missing required argument, for which the agent prompts the user, in 86.2-93.7% of cases (Fig. 4b). In 2-6 cases per agent, they filled missing required value with another value written in the request, which represents wrong choice, not an invention. The LLM-based agents behaved correctly in at most 5.7% of cases. They mostly answered without call or filled the missing value with an invented one in up to 62.1% of underspecified requests. Even the most accurate LLM setting invented the missing value in 27.6% of them  (Table 1)  . System 1 agents declined 87.0-94.5% of the 307 outof-scope requests and left 1.0-3.3% of complete requests without call (Fig. 4c). The LLM-based agents declined 41.4-97.4% and left 0.0-36.5% without call. The two that declined most, left 24.3% and 36.5% of complete requests without call. Of the three kinds of out-ofscope request, those for which tool performs the task but not on the given input were the hardest for every agent. In 22 of the 10,888 System 1 calls, value written in the request was placed where the schema requires another form, such as an identifier pattern. The LLMbased agents made such calls at similar rate  (Table 1)  . Efficiency. System 1 agents used 0.072-0.407 Wh of GPU energy per fully correct request, against 0.1982.481 Wh for LLM-based agents with reasoning and 0.080-0.853 Wh without (Fig. 5 and Extended Data Table 6). request took 1.2-10.1 with System 1, in comparison to 2.6-26.1 for LLM-based agents with reasoning and 1.1-9.2 without. At the top of the accuracy range, OpenJev-based System 1 agent was fully correct on 92.9% of requests, with 2.6 per request and 0.228 Wh per fully correct request, against 91.3%, 4.5 and 0.413 Wh for the best LLM-based agent setting. System 1 agent asked about 12 questions per request and generated no text, whereas the LLM-based agents generated 123-340 tokens per request without reasoning and 417-952 with it. All agents fitted on one 48-GB GPU, with peak GPU memory of 7,368-35,057 MiB for System 1 agents and 12,044-45,532 MiB for LLM-based agents. Robustness and reproducibility. The comparison was independent of the value-matching method. Two values were considered equivalent when they would have been treated as equivalent by the server, for example, through its own name-matching table (Methods). However, the servers did not resolve equivalence in two cases: stop words, such as and or the, in database search text, and model names that an AutoML server passed directly to its underlying library. To assess the sensitivity of the results to these choices, we rescored all agents using the alternative matching rule for each case. Search text was compared exactly as written, while model names System 1 agents 4 were matched using the librarys own name table. The first alternative did not change any pairwise comparisons. The second changed one of the 324 comparisons from System 1 advantage to no statistically significant difference (Extended Data Table 8). The comparison was also independent of the reasoning mode. For fully correct requests, System 1 agents outperformed the LLM-based agents in 37 of the 54 pairs with reasoning enabled, while the LLM-based agents performed better in 6. With reasoning disabled, the corresponding counts were 36 and 5. When each LLMbased agent was evaluated using its better-performing mode, selected retrospectively based on the results, choice that favored the LLMs, System 1 agent still outperformed the LLM-based agent in 33 of 54 pairs, compared with 8 in which the LLM-based agent performed better. The advantage was also not limited to generated requests. On the 123 prompts taken verbatim from the notebooks of two published agent systems, System 1 agents achieved mean tool-calling and argument-filling accuracy at least as high as that of LLM agents in either reasoning mode (Extended Data Table 5). Every result can be traced to the released data (Data availability). Replaying the stored decision-model answers through the released code rebuilds all 12,756 System 1 records of the evaluation set. Rescoring each System 1 record from its recorded call reproduced its stored verdict, and rescoring the LLM completions reproduced the totals of the run summaries of all 18 LLMagent settings. The released scripts can be used to regenerate every figure, Table 1, Extended Data Tables 3-8 and every statistic in the text.

sections.title: DISCUSSION
sections.content: Clinical and other sensitive data call for agents that run locally and do not invent content. Current options force trade-off. Cloud LLMs are capable but move data off site. Local LLMs keep data on site but, as we show, put invented values into 5.5-19.7% of their tool calls and invent missing required values for up to 62.1% of underspecified requests. In pipeline, each such value silently changes the analysis and every step that follows. System 1 agents remove this trade-off for tool calling. They run on local GPU and cannot hallucinate content, because they never generate text. Every tool, argument and value in call is chosen from options that come from the catalogue, the request, the schema or the agents policy. We observed no invented content in 10,888 calls. When required value is missing, they leave it empty and prompt the user for it with template built from the schema. Every decision carries probability and every run can be replayed, which makes the behaviour of the agent auditable. These properties did not cost accuracy. The two strongest System 1 agents were ahead of every local LLM setting or level with the best one, mainly because they chose tools and declined more reliably. On average they were faster and used less energy than LLM-based agents with reasoning, although Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with reasoning used less energy than OpenJev-based System 1 agent. At the top of the accuracy range, OpenJevbased System 1 agent was faster and cheaper than the best LLM setting. The decision model mattered since the two pplx-decider System 1 models were better tool callers than their base model run as an agent, whereas decider-35b-a3b was not. System 1 agents are not error-free. They still make wrong choices among grounded options. In limited number of cases, they picked wrong tools, put written values into the wrong argument and, in 22 of 10,888 calls, sent grounded text in form the schema rejects. Checking each option against the arguments schema, pattern and type, before offering it would remove the last of these. Requests for which tool performs the task but not on the given input were hard for every agent. On argument filling, five LLM-based agents were not significantly different from the best System 1 agent. In conclusion, herein we present general method to develop System 1 agents. As scientific and clinical tools adopt common interfaces such as MCP, System 1 agents offer route to local, reliable and fast automation of analyses on sensitive data, in which every step is grounded, scored and auditable. METHODS Decision models. decision model maps state, question and list of options to probability distribution over the options, in one forward pass and without sampling. We used six published models from three protocol families, unchanged and without fine-tuning (Extended Data Table 1) 1417. Each was served by llama.cpp (build b11929) 23 entirely on one GPU, with one request slot; every question was its own request. Decider family models (decider-4b, decider-35b-a3b). The prompt is the familys state-first layout, built as token ids with the checkpoints tokenizer: context block with the state, the question, the options labelled (A), (B), . . . and an answer prefix. The answer is read at the final position. The log-probabilities of the option-label tokens returned by llama-server before sampling, are divided by the models fitted temperature and normalized over the valid labels. Up to ten options use the letters A-J and larger questions use one single-token label per option, up to 255. pplx-decider family models (pplx-decider-flash, pplxdecider-27b). The prompt is the checkpoints chat template around fixed system prompt and user turn with the state, the question and the options, ending in marker token. The models full-attention layers are non-causal. llama-server runs in embeddings mode and returns the final hidden state at the marker. The agent applies the models read-out matrix (255 hidden size) and temperature and normalizes over the options. We verified this path against the reference implementation System 1 agents on the 4B model. Native SystemOne models (OpenJev, Clef). llama.cpp implements their prompt, read-out head and temperatures. Its /v1/systemone endpoint takes the state and one question whose criteria are the option texts and returns one probability per option. OpenJev takes at most 52 options per question. Larger questions are split into balanced groups. The model answers within each group and then among the group winners, and an options probability is the product of its group winners final probability and its probability within the group. Determinism and stored answers. For given model, hardware and llama.cpp build, the same state, question, options and kind give the same distribution. Every answer was stored under the SHA-256 hash of (model, kind, state, question, options). Compiler. The compiler turns one tools input schema and the request into questions, sends them to the decision model and assembles the answers into argument values. Argument kinds. Each property gets kind from its type, name and description: enumeration, boolean, number, path, column, free text, list, array of arrays or object. union type (anyOf or oneOf, such as Optional[X]) is read as its single non-null type. Questions. The state of every question is the request, the tools name and description, and any earlier steps. An enumeration is asked as Which value should the argument take? over its values, plus not specified in the request (keep the default) for an optional argument. boolean is asked as Does the request turn the option on or off? over on, off and, if optional, not mentioned. Numbers, paths, columns and free text use the value question over their candidates plus not specified. List items are picked one at time over the remaining candidates plus no further item. Written arrays and dictionaries are offered whole, otherwise an object is filled through yes/no question, its keys and one value question per key. Candidates. Candidates come from four sources. (1) The request: paths, numbers in digits or words, ranges, quoted strings, identifiers and compact codes, phrases of up to three words for name and search arguments, written lists and dictionaries, and text after label. (2) Forms derived from the request for arguments that take them: unit conversions, fractions and percentages, class counts, dataset identifiers, chromosome and allele notations, and paths composed from written parts. (3) The schema: values description lists and documented list items. (4) The environment and earlier steps: the header of CSV file another argument points to, and earlier results. Words that name the tool or its server are not offered. Settling and acceptance. Independent questions are sent together and settle in fixed order: free values settle highest probability first, so written value goes to the argument that wants it most. value fills at most as many arguments as the request writes it. Used values stay visible but cannot be picked again. When two arguments claim the same value, the model is asked which argument the value belongs to, and that answer decides only if its probability reaches 0.7. An optional argument is set only when the probability on its allowed values reaches 0.7, and lists first item must reach 0.7. value equal to the documented default is not passed. required argument without value is reported as missing, and one answered below 0.5 as uncertain. Agent. The agent state consisted of the current user request and all preceding steps. Tool selection was performed through multiple-choice question that included all available tools, each represented by its server and name followed by the first 220 characters of its description, as well as none of these option for requests that could not be handled by any available tool. When the two most probable tools had selection probabilities within 0.3 of each other, second question presented the two tools and their parameter names to determine which tool had parameters corresponding to the values specified in the request. subsequent yes/no question presented the selected tools full description and parameter names to assess whether it could fulfil the request. The agent declined requests when the probability of positive answer was below 0.5. In deployment, the agent also declined when its selection confidence, calculated as the product of the probabilities assigned to the steps, fell below 0.3. This threshold was not applied during evaluation, so declines resulted only from selecting none of these or failing the capability check. When required argument was missing or uncertain, the agent presented the user with fixed prompt containing the argument name and the first 120 characters of its schema description, and used the value provided by the user. If the request did not specify an output folder, the agent populated this argument according to predefined policy. Because the evaluation was conducted without user interaction, the agent instead listed missing arguments in its plan. An underspecified request was considered correctly handled when this list contained exactly the arguments labelled as missing. For multi-step requests, each tool call and the first 1,200 characters of its result were added to the agent state. The agent then used an additional question to determine whether another step was required. Development method. All development was confined to the compiler and agent and was conducted exclusively on development requests. First, every textual value required by tool call was presented to the model as an option, while operations that could be performed exactly through code were handled by the compiler. Second, compiler oracle replaced the decision model with component that selected the labelled value whenever System 1 agents 6 it was available. This provided measure of which labelled calls could be expressed by the compiler. Third, each failure was classified as compiler failure, model failure or labelling error. Compiler failures occurred when value was not offered or was offered in an incorrect form. Model failures occurred when an offered value was not selected. Only compiler failures were addressed. Fourth, each modification introduced general rule governing how requests expressed values or how schemas described arguments, rather than toolspecific rule. Its acceptance criteria were documented before any model was evaluated against it. Fifth, set of modifications was retained only if it increased the aggregate number of fully correct calls across models on the development requests, did not cause any earlier reference request to fall beyond predefined tolerance, and could not be simplified by removing an individual modification without increasing the aggregate score. Sixth, stored model responses made repeated evaluations inexpensive and exactly reproducible. Seventh, the code and configuration were hashed before the test evaluation. Tools and catalogues. catalogue is JSON snapshot of each servers tool list: every tools name, description and input schema as the server returns it. The tested 157 tools were indexed in two catalogues: (i) the imaging catalogue with 42 tools of 11 MCP servers 24: 2D and 3D image classification, nnUNet 21, the Merlin CT foundation model 25, PyCaret 26 classification and regression, exploratory data analysis, feature importance, model comparison, PyRadiomics 27 and TotalSegmentator 28 (ii) the biomedical catalogue has 115 tools of 7 MCP servers: proteomicsmcp (53 tools), AlphaGenome 29 (22), MSMCP (13), ClinicalTrials.gov (7), ChEMBL 22 (7), Scanpy 30 (7) and TISSUE (6). The AlphaGenome, Scanpy and TISSUE servers come from Paper2Agent 3, and the ClinicalTrials.gov and ChEMBL servers from CyanHeads (https://github.com/cyanheads/chembl-mcp-server). Prompt Requests, labels and evaluation set. Prompt requests were designed to resemble explicit, researcherstyle instructions and to cover range of linguistic and numerical phenomena, including paraphrasing, distractor values, alternative number formats, quotation, negation and textual noise. Out-of-scope requests covered three categories: far, referring to tasks unrelated to the available tools, near, referring to related tasks for which no available tool provided the required functionality, and modality, referring to tasks supported by an available tool but not for the specified input type. Each request was labelled with the tool whose execution would fulfil it and no tool for out-of-scope requests. Labels included only argument values explicitly stated in the request and represented in forms accepted by the corresponding server. Values not specified in the request, values requiring external knowledge and values appearing only in schema examples were excluded. Requests that required tool but omitted mandatory argument were classified as underspecified, with the missing arguments recorded in their labels. The evaluation set comprised 2,126 requests: 2,003 custom prompts (1,179 for the imaging catalogue and 824 for the biomedical catalogue) and 123 prompts taken verbatim from published research studies (73 from ReclAIm 19 and 50 from mAIstro 20, both for the imaging catalogue). All 123 published prompts are complete requests. The evaluation set therefore contains 1,645 complete requests (1,522 custom and 123 published) specifying 6,056 argument values (5,467 and 589), 307 out-of-scope requests that could not be handled by any available tool and 174 underspecified requests that omitted at least one required argument; all out-of-scope and underspecified requests are custom. The 1,952 complete and out-of-scope requests (1,829 custom and 123 published) form the main benchmark, on which tool calling, argument filling and fully correct requests are measured. The 174 underspecified requests are evaluated separately. LLM agents. Nine open-weight LLMs served as the core reasoning engine of the LLM-based agents (Extended Data Table 2). The request was the only user message, with no specific system prompt. Each request received one completion (seed 20261102, at most 16,384 generated tokens), and no tool was executed. llama.cpp (build b11929) parsed tool calls with its native parser. The first call was scored, and an answer without call counted as decline. Each model ran with reasoning on and off through its chat template. Muse Glimmer 30B has no off setting, so its lowest level stood for off. Scoring. scoring tool was developed to evaluate every agent. Tool calling was considered correct when the labelled tool was called for complete request or no tool was selected for an out-of-scope request. Argumentfilling accuracy was calculated as the proportion of labelled values that were correctly provided in calls to the correct tool. request was considered fully correct when the correct tool was called, all labelled values were provided correctly and no required value was missing, or when an out-of-scope request was declined. Values were compared as received by the server. Case differences were ignored, comma-separated lists were compared as sets, numerical values were compared numerically, and values that server mapped to the same entry through its own name-matching table were considered equivalent. For ClinicalTrials.gov, the scorer applied the server's own normalisation procedures, whereas for ChEMBL it used the server's assaytype codes. Search text was compared after removing English stop words 31, irrespective of word order. Two matching rules were determined by the scorer. Their sensitivity was assessed by repeating all pairwise comparisons under alternative rules. First, search text System 1 agents 7 was compared exactly as provided, without removing stop words. Second, model names passed by the PyCaret regression server, which did not have its own namematching table, were matched using PyCaret's table of model identifiers and names rather than compared as written. Values not specified in the request were not counted as errors, but were reported separately. String values corresponding to an argument's declared type were converted in the same way as schema-validating server would convert them. For underspecified requests, correct behaviour required calling the correct tool, providing all stated values correctly and leaving the missing required arguments unfilled. Fabricated content. For every call in the evaluation set, we recorded four types of errors: (i) the use of nonexistent tool, defined as function absent from the tool catalogue, (ii) the use of nonexistent argument, defined as an argument name absent from the schema of the selected tool, (iii) the inclusion of an invented value and (iv) for underspecified requests, the filling of missing required argument. value, including string, number, list item, object key or object value, was considered grounded if it matched labelled value, appeared in the request text (ignoring differences in case, spaces, underscores, hyphens and slashes), was number explicitly stated in the request, was an option offered by the compiler for that argument and request, or appeared in the tool schema. Booleans, empty values and the output folder were excluded from this assessment. Values that violated the schema's type or pattern constraints were recorded separately as schema-validity errors. Local deployment. All inference ran on one workstation with one GPU, through local llama.cpp servers. No request, tool schema or answer was sent to an external service during the runs and the scorers normalizers also run locally. Inference was performed on machine with an NVIDIA RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell GPU (48 GB), 32 CPU threads and 62 GB of memory under Ubuntu 24.04. Time and energy. For each request we recorded wallclock time, prompt and generated tokens, GPU energy from the NVML total-energy counter of the whole board, mean power, utilization and peak memory. Idle power was measured for 20 with the model loaded before each run. Energy per fully correct request is the GPU energy over the 1,952 (1,645 complete and 307 outof-scope) main requests divided by the number fully correct. Statistics. Each System 1 agent was compared with each LLM-based agent in each reasoning mode (108 pairs per measure). Tool calling and fully correct requests were compared with the exact two-sided McNemar test on discordant requests and argument filling with an exact two-sided paired sign-flip test on perrequest differences in right values. P-values were adjusted with Holms method over the 108 pairs of each measure, with significance at an adjusted < 0.05. Fully correct requests are the primary measure; both reasoning modes are co-primary. Same-backbone comparisons are reported with unadjusted P-values. Proportions have 95% Wilson intervals and argument filling has 95% percentile intervals from 4,000 bootstrap resamples of requests.
